notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on 2 Samuel 13, drawn from the sources I was able to access within the allotted searches and fetches.

---

## 2 Samuel 13 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1
"After some time" marks the general period following David's sin with Bathsheba and the Ammonite war. Absalom and Tamar were children of David through Maacah, daughter of Talmai king of Geshur (2 Sam 3:3). Amnon was David's firstborn, son of Ahinoam the Jezreelitess (2 Sam 3:2). His "love" for Tamar was not honourable love aiming at marriage but lustful desire. Gill notes that Amnon "loved her" not to make her his wife but "in a lustful manner, to make an harlot of her."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-13/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-13.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-13.html
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/2_samuel/13.htm

### v. 2
Amnon was "sick with frustration" — the Hebrew conveys that he was distressed, straitened, and pined away with ungoverned passion (Gill, Ellicott). The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Hebrew literally means "it became narrow (anxious) to Amnon, even to making himself ill," i.e., he quite pined away — not pretending illness yet (that comes later). The phrase "she was a virgin" explains why Amnon found it impossible to get near her: the modest seclusion of Tamar in the harem raised an insuperable barrier. Ellicott comments that "it seemed impossible to Amnon" to carry out his desires because the king's children lived in separate households.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-13.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-13.html
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/kad/2_samuel/13.htm

### v. 3
Jonadab was the son of Shimeah (called Shammah in 1 Sam 16:9), David's brother — making him Amnon's cousin. He is described as "a very shrewd/crafty man" (Hebrew *subtil*). Ellicott notes the word indicates "sagacity and wisdom, whether rightly or wrongly exercised." Trapp (quoted in Enduring Word) calls him "a friend no friend; a carnal friend, a spiritual enemy, who advised, for the recovery of the body, the ruin of his soul." Clarke calls Jonadab's advice "most diabolic."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-13/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-13.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-13.html

### v. 4
Jonadab noticed Amnon looking "lean from day to day" (literally "morning by morning") and pressed him to confess. Amnon answered, "I love Tamar, my brother Absalom's sister." Gill notes Amnon does not call her "my sister" but "Absalom's sister," to lessen the sense of his unlawful love. Enduring Word emphasizes that lust was already twisting how Amnon saw reality — he would not call Tamar his own sister.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-13/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-13.html

### v. 5
Jonadab's crafty plan: feign sickness, ask David to send Tamar to prepare food "in my sight" so Amnon could "eat from her hand." Ellicott distinguishes this feigned sickness from the real pining of v. 2: "That was the real pining of ungoverned and ungratified passion; this was a crafty feigning of sickness. Yet the miserable condition to which Amnon was brought by the former would give colour and plausibility to the latter." Jonadab also directed Amnon to call her "my sister Tamar" (not "Absalom's sister"), the more to cover his ill design (Gill).

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-13.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-13.html

### v. 6
Amnon followed the scheme exactly. David came to see his supposedly sick son. Amnon requested Tamar make "a couple of cakes" (*heart cakes*, Gill notes — possibly called so for their form or for their comforting effect). Enduring Word observes that Amnon's behaviour was "clearly childish, and David indulged it." This indulgence by David is a theme throughout the commentaries.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-13/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-13.html

### v. 7
David "sent word to Tamar at the palace." Ellicott notes the Hebrew is literally "into the house," meaning the private apartments of the women — the harem. David unknowingly facilitated the crime by commanding Tamar to go.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-13.html

### vv. 8–9
Tamar came innocently, kneaded dough, made cakes and baked them in Amnon's sight, exactly as requested. Then Amnon refused to eat and ordered everyone out — behaviour that "awakened no suspicion in the mind of Tamar" because it seemed natural for a "whimsical invalid" (Ellicott). Gill notes the pretense was that company troubled him and he needed rest.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-13.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-13.html

### vv. 10–11
Amnon called Tamar into the bedroom (inner chamber) for more privacy. When she brought the food, "he took hold of her and said, 'Come lie with me, my sister.'" Gill observes: "One would think the relation he observes she stood in to him would have checked him from making so vile a motion." Enduring Word calls Amnon "a spoiled prince who always took what he wanted."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-13/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-13.html

### v. 12
Tamar resisted with moral reasoning: "No such thing ought to be done in Israel. Do not do this disgraceful thing!" ("folly" in older translations). Ellicott notes she quoted "the very words of Genesis 34:7," appealing to Israel's traditions to recall the king's son to a sense of right. Tamar used the strongest moral language: "do not force me" (rape), "disgraceful thing" (Hebrew *nebalah* — a term for serious disorderly and unruly conduct, noted by Constable). Gill: Tamar urged "the honour of religion, and the reputation of Israel, and the glory of the God of Israel."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-13.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-13.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-13.html

### v. 13
Tamar continued pleading: "Where could I ever take my shame? And you would be like one of the fools in Israel!" Then she suggested, "Please speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you." Commentators differ on whether Tamar believed this was possible. Ellicott argues the Law (Lev 18:9, 11; 20:17) strictly forbade half-sibling marriage, and Tamar "made any and every suggestion to gain time and escape the pressing danger." Enduring Word concurs: "Tamar probably said this simply as a ploy to get away from Amnon." Gill, however, notes some rabbinic traditions that suggested she might have been born of a captive woman before proselytisation, making her technically free for Amnon — though he adds she likely "said this, and anything that occurred to her mind, to put him off."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-13.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-13.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-13/

### v. 14
Amnon "would not heed her voice; and being stronger than she, he forced her and lay with her." The NET Bible notes the Hebrew verbs: "he humiliated her and lay with her." Constable contrasts the Hebrew verbs used here (*shakab 'et* — to lie with, implying force) with David's sin (*shakab 'im* — to sleep with, implying some degree of consent). This was unequivocally rape.

- https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=2sa+13%3A1-39
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-13.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-13/

### v. 15
"Then Amnon hated Tamar with such intensity that his hatred was greater than the love he previously had." This sudden reversal is widely noted by commentators as proof that Amnon's "love" was pure lust. Ellicott quotes Tacitus: "It is characteristic of human nature to hate one whom you have injured." Enduring Word: "Tamar was simply a reminder of his foolish sin. He wanted every reminder of his sin to be put far away." Constable contrasts this with pagan Shechem who, after violating Dinah (Gen 34), "loved" her — Amnon's reaction was far worse.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-13.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-13/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-13.html

### v. 16
Tamar protested: "Sending me away is worse than this great wrong you have already done to me!" Ellicott explains: "Amnon was now doing her a greater wrong than at first, because he was now bound, in consequence of that, to protect and comfort her." Under Exodus 22:16–17 and Deuteronomy 22:28–29, a man who violated a virgin was required to pay a bride-price and marry her (if the father permitted). Sending her away compounded the wrong by making her publicly disgraced. Gill notes that the secret sin could have been hidden, but open expulsion exposed her to shame.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-13.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-13.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-13/

### v. 17
Amnon called his attendant: "Throw this woman out and bolt the door behind her!" Ellicott comments that Amnon "doubtless intended to give the impression that Tamar had behaved shamefully towards him. The baseness of this insinuation is in keeping with his brutality." Gill observes that Amnon used the contemptuous "this woman" rather than calling her by name or acknowledging her as his sister.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-13.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-13.html

### v. 18
Tamar was wearing a "robe of many colors" (Hebrew *ketonet passim*), the special garment worn by the king's virgin daughters. The NET Bible notes this is the same rare Hebrew phrase used for Joseph's coat in Genesis 37:3, and likely refers to a long-sleeved tunic reaching the wrists and ankles — a garment of privilege and status showing the wearer did not have to do manual labour. Ellicott says the mention shows that Tamar would have been immediately recognised as a royal virgin by the servant who cast her out.

- https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=2sa+13%3A1-39
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-13.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-13/

### v. 19
Tamar put ashes on her head, tore her royal robe, placed her hand on her head, and went away "crying bitterly." These are classic biblical gestures of extreme mourning and distress (cf. Joshua 7:6, Jeremiah 2:37). Gaebelein (from Precept Austin) notes the hand on the head is "the oriental way of expressing a heavy burden." Enduring Word emphasizes: "She did not give place to the voice of shame saying, 'This was somehow your fault.'"

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-13/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-13-commentary
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-13.html

### v. 20
Absalom immediately guessed what happened: "Has your brother Amnon been with you?" Then he said, "Be quiet for now, my sister. He is your brother. Do not take this thing to heart." Ellicott notes Absalom "counsels silence as necessary to the purpose of revenge he had at once formed." Gill adds that Absalom spoke "not out of love of Amnon, but as desirous of gratifying private revenge." Tamar "lived as a desolate woman" (literally "remained desolate") in Absalom's house — she never married and lived in disgrace.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-13.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-13.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-13/

### v. 21
"When King David heard all this, he was furious" — but notably he did nothing. This is a major point in all the commentaries. **An important textual note:** the Septuagint (LXX), Vulgate, and Josephus add: "But he would not grieve the spirit of Amnon his son, for he loved him, because he was his firstborn." This addition is attested by Clarke, the NET Bible notes, Ellicott, and Constable. Matthew Henry sums up the traditional reading: David was "too indulgent to his children." Gaebelein suggests David's own past sin "maimed his arm" for discipline. Constable: "How can a father discipline his children when he knows that he has done worse than they?" Meyer (quoted in Enduring Word): "They say a man never hears his own voice till it comes back to him from the phonograph."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-13.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-13.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-13/
- https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=2sa+13%3A1-39
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-13-commentary

### v. 22
"Absalom never said a word to Amnon, either good or bad, because he hated Amnon." Gill notes the Hebrew *ki* can be read as "though" — i.e., *though* Absalom hated Amnon, he behaved with outward friendliness to avoid suspicion while plotting revenge. Trapp (quoted in Enduring Word): "Nothing is more unsafe to be trusted, than the fair looks of a festered heart."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-13/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-13.html

### vv. 23–24
"Two full years" passed. Absalom's silent hatred festered. Sheepshearing was a festive occasion (cf. 1 Sam 25:2). Baal-hazor was near Ephraim, probably northeast of Jerusalem (Gill, citing Reland and Eusebius, places Ephraim about eight miles from Jerusalem). Absalom invited "all the sons of the king" and pressed David himself to come — a calculated move to "disguise his real purpose" and secure David's blessing (Ellicott).

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-13.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-samuel-13.html

### vv. 25–27
David declined to go ("we should not all go, or we would be a burden to you") but gave his blessing. Absalom then specifically asked for Amnon. David asked, "Why should he go with you?" — a moment of hesitation. Ellicott comments that David "could not well refuse without acknowledging a suspicion which he was unwilling to express, he finally consents." The LXX adds at the end of v. 27: "And Absalom made a feast like the feast of a king."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-13.html

### v. 28
Absalom commanded his servants to wait until Amnon's "heart is merry with wine," then strike him down. He told them: "Do not be afraid. Have I not commanded you? Be courageous and valiant!" Constable notes a grim parallel: "As David had committed adultery, made Uriah drunk, and then murdered him: so Amnon committeth incest, is made drunk, and [is] then murdered" (Trapp, quoted in Enduring Word). Ellicott notes the servants would have followed the prince's orders without question, leaving responsibility with Absalom. If Chileab (Daniel) was already dead, Absalom stood next in succession after Amnon.

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-13/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-13.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-13.html

### v. 29
The servants killed Amnon. All the other king's sons fled, "each one on his mule." Ellicott notes the mule was ridden by persons of distinction (cf. 2 Sam 18:9; 1 Kgs 1:33). Though mule-breeding was forbidden in the Law (Lev 19:19), mules were imported through commerce (1 Kgs 10:25).

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-13.html

### vv. 30–31
A false (exaggerated) report reached David: "Absalom has struck down all the sons of the king; not one of them is left!" Ellicott calls this "so true to the life" and evidence of "contemporaneous authorship." David tore his clothes, lay on the ground, and all his servants stood by with torn clothes. Enduring Word notes: "It is significant that David did not react to this news with disbelief. He sensed that Absalom was capable of such evil."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-13.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-13/

### vv. 32–33
Jonadab — the same man who had given Amnon the wicked advice — now appeared to "comfort" David with the news that only Amnon was dead. He even revealed that "Absalom has planned this since the day Amnon violated his sister Tamar." Enduring Word notes: "Jonadab probably hoped to gain favor with David by bringing this more favorable news, but God knew that Jonadab set the whole course of events in motion." Matthew Henry minces no words: "Jonadab was as guilty of Ammon's death, as of his sin; such false friends do they prove, who counsel us to do wickedly." Gaebelein calls Jonadab "one of the most abominable characters in Bible history."

- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-13/
- https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/2_samuel/13.htm
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-13-commentary

### vv. 34–36
Absalom fled. The watchman saw "many people coming down the road west of him" (literally "behind him," the orienting direction being east). The king's sons arrived "wailing loudly," and David and all his servants "wept very bitterly." Enduring Word comments: "David is rightly grieved at learning of the death of his eldest son, the Crown Prince Amnon. Yet David's lack of correction of Amnon contributed to this murder."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-13.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-13/

### vv. 37–38
Absalom fled to Talmai son of Ammihud, king of Geshur — his maternal grandfather (2 Sam 3:3). He stayed there three years. David "mourned for his son every day" — the son mourned being Amnon (Ellicott). Enduring Word notes that Absalom did not go to a city of refuge because he was guilty of murder, and cities of refuge were only for the innocent (cf. Num 35; Deut 19).

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-13.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-13/

### v. 39
"And King David longed to go to Absalom, for he had been consoled over Amnon's death." This verse is famously difficult and disputed. The Hebrew is ambiguous. The traditional English reading (KJV, and reflected in the BSB) takes it as David longing *for* Absalom — that his grief for Amnon had subsided, and he now pined for Absalom's return. This is the view of the Chaldee (Targum) and Jewish commentators, per Ellicott.

However, Ellicott himself argues for the **alternative interpretation**: taking the verb impersonally, the sense is "David *desisted from going forth against* Absalom." That is, David should have punished Absalom for the murder (which was both fratricide and high treason as assassination of the heir-apparent), but with time he "was comforted concerning Amnon" and gradually gave up the thought of punishing Absalom. Ellicott gives three reasons: (1) there is no ground for supplying "the soul of" in the ellipsis; (2) the verb never elsewhere has the sense of "longing"; and (3) David could easily have recalled Absalom if he had wanted to, yet when Absalom was actually brought back, David refused to see him for two more years (2 Sam 14:24, 28).

The NET Bible translation notes adopt a similar view: "The king longed to go to Absalom" (following 4QSamᵃ and reading "the spirit of the king" rather than MT "David the king"), understanding it as David's abiding love for Absalom despite alienation.

Enduring Word takes the traditional reading: "David simply longed to be reconciled to Absalom again — without correcting his son for his evil. David's indulgence towards Amnon is repeated towards Absalom and he will meet a similar end."

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-13.html
- https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=2sa+13%3A1-39
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-13/

## Points of Difference Between Traditions

Due to search limits, I could not access separate pages for each denominational tradition. However, the sources I retrieved do represent a range of perspectives and some differences can be noted:

### The Septuagint Addition at v. 21
The LXX (and Vulgate, and Josephus) adds to v. 21: "But he would not grieve the spirit of Amnon his son, for he loved him, because he was his firstborn." This is noted by **Clarke** (Methodist/Wesleyan), **Ellicott** (Anglican), **NET Bible notes** (modern scholarship), and **Constable** (evangelical). Some modern Catholic Bibles (like the NAB) include this addition. Traditional Protestant Bibles (KJV, ESV, NASB) follow the shorter Hebrew Masoretic Text. The addition helps explain David's inaction, but its absence from the MT raises text-critical questions.

- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-samuel-13.html
- https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=2sa+13%3A1-39

### The Translation of v. 39
As noted above, the traditional reading (David "longed to go to" Absalom) vs. the impersonal reading (David "desisted from going out against" Absalom) represents a significant exegetical divide. The traditional reading is held by older Protestant commentators (Matthew Henry, Gill, Pulpit) and is followed by Enduring Word (Pentecostal/charismatic). The alternative reading is championed by Ellicott (Anglican) and discussed favourably in the NET Bible (modern evangelical scholarship).

### Amnon's and Absalom's Sins as Fulfillment of Nathan's Prophecy
Virtually all Protestant traditions (Baptist, Reformed, Methodist, Pentecostal) read this chapter as the direct outworking of 2 Samuel 12:10–11 — "the sword shall never depart from your house." The parallel between David's sins (adultery, making Uriah drunk, murder) and his sons' sins (rape/incest, making Amnon drunk, murder) is widely noted. Gaebelein (Plymouth Brethren/evangelical): "Pardoned he was, but the harvest is on. What a man soweth that he will reap." Precept Austin: "This chapter describes the firstfruits of David's sins of adultery and murder." Constable (Dallas Theological Seminary): "David's sons were chips off the old block."

- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-13-commentary
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-13.html

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship (NET Bible)
The NET Bible notes provide technical detail: the Hitpael stem of the verb in vv. 2 and 5 describes "making oneself appear to be of a certain character" (real sickness in v. 2, feigned in v. 5). The phrase "robe of many colors" (*ketonet passim*) is only found here and in Genesis 37; the LXX translation *chitōna poikilon* ("garment of divers colors") may not be accurate — it likely means a long-sleeved robe reaching to wrists and ankles. The NET Bible also notes the textual variant in v. 39 (4QSamᵃ reads "the spirit of the king" rather than MT "David the king").

- https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=2sa+13%3A1-39

### Catholic and Orthodox
I was unable to access Catholic-specific (newadvent.org, catholic.com) or Orthodox (oca.org) commentaries directly due to search limits. The references to the LXX addition at v. 21 (preserved in the Vulgate and thus in Catholic Bibles) represent the most notable point of difference. Catholic commentaries typically include this longer reading and consequently offer a more explicit explanation for David's failure to discipline Amnon: his doting love for his firstborn son.

### Debated Popular Modern Teaching
No specific prosperity, Word of Faith, or hyper-grace teaching on 2 Samuel 13 was found in the sources searched.
